clauses.text: This policy explains how {ORG} uses artificial intelligence (AI) tools, including generative AI. Its purpose is to let staff and volunteers benefit from these tools while protecting the people we serve, our supporters, and our mission.
This policy applies to all staff, volunteers, board members, contractors, and interns whenever they use AI tools for {ORG} work, on any device or account.

"AI tools" here means any software that generates content, makes predictions, or produces recommendations — including chat assistants, writing and image generators, transcription and translation tools, and AI features built into software we already use.

AI use at {ORG} follows three principles: people remain responsible for every work product; the privacy and dignity of the people we serve come before convenience; and we are honest about when and how we use AI.
This policy works alongside our existing policies, including confidentiality, data protection, and codes of conduct. Where policies overlap, the stricter rule applies.
Nothing in this policy requires anyone to use AI. Choosing not to use AI for a task is always acceptable. Concerns about AI use can be raised with {OWNER_ROLE} without any negative consequences.
{ORG} adopts this policy as part of the board's oversight of organizational risk. Management reports significant AI-related issues and material changes in AI use to the board.
{ORG} takes a cautious approach to AI. Tools and uses are permitted only when this policy or {OWNER_ROLE} explicitly approves them; anything not approved is not permitted.

{ORG} encourages thoughtful experimentation with AI within the guardrails in this policy. If a use is not addressed here and involves no sensitive data, staff may try it and are asked to share what they learn.
AI tools may be used for drafting and editing documents, emails, and communications, provided a person reviews the output before it is used or sent.
AI tools may be used for brainstorming, outlining, summarizing publicly available information, and getting unstuck on a first draft.
Whoever uses an AI tool owns the result. AI output is a starting point; the staff member who submits, sends, or publishes it is responsible for its accuracy, fairness, and tone.

For external communications — newsletters, appeals, reports, web copy — AI may draft, but a person must fact-check every claim, verify every name and number, and make sure the voice is genuinely ours.

AI may assist with grant research and proposal drafting. Statements about our programs, results, and finances must be verified against our own records before submission, and funders' rules about AI-assisted applications must be checked and followed.

AI may support fundraising work such as drafting appeals and researching publicly available information about institutional funders. It may not be used to compile intrusive profiles of individual donors or to fabricate personalization that implies a relationship we do not have.
AI may be used to analyze aggregated or de-identified data, draft queries, and explore trends. Conclusions that will inform decisions must be checked by someone who understands the underlying data.

AI transcription and meeting-notes tools may be used only with the knowledge of meeting participants, and never in conversations where confidential client matters are discussed unless the tool has been approved for that purpose.
Translation tools may be used for internal understanding and drafts. Client-facing or legally significant translations must be reviewed by a qualified person before use.

AI-generated images and audio may be used for illustration with appropriate rights review. They may never depict real clients, staff, or events in a way that could be mistaken for photography or recordings of real events without clear labeling.
Code and automation written with AI assistance must be reviewed and tested like any other code before it touches production systems or real data.
Never enter confidential, sensitive, or personally identifying information about clients, donors, staff, or volunteers into an AI tool that has not been approved for that category of data.
Never present AI output as settled fact without verification. AI tools produce confident errors; publishing one under our name damages the trust our mission depends on.
Never use AI to impersonate a real person, fabricate quotes, testimonials, or endorsements, or create misleading images or recordings of real people or events.

AI may not make final decisions about individual people — including clients, beneficiaries, applicants, or employees. A qualified person must make and own any decision that affects an individual's services, application, or employment.

In hiring and HR, AI may help draft job descriptions and organize processes. It may not screen out candidates, evaluate individuals, or influence employment decisions without documented human review of each affected person's case.
Do not use AI tools to generate legal, medical, tax, or clinical advice for clients or the public. AI may help staff prepare materials, but professional advice must come from qualified professionals.
Do not upload documents we hold under confidentiality obligations — contracts, personnel records, board materials marked confidential, or partner data — to unapproved tools.

Do not use AI to scrape, harvest, or infer sensitive characteristics about individuals — such as health status, immigration status, religion, or sexual orientation — whether or not the underlying data is technically public.
Do not connect AI tools to our systems, data, or accounts through plug-ins, integrations, or agents without approval from {OWNER_ROLE}.
Client and beneficiary information of any kind, identified or not, may not be entered into any AI tool unless {OWNER_ROLE} has approved that specific tool for that specific purpose in writing.
Treat every AI tool as a third party. Before entering any information, ask: would we email this content to an outside company? If not, do not enter it.
Data entered into consumer AI tools may be stored and used to train future models. Assume anything entered into an unapproved tool leaves our control permanently.

Donor names, contact details, giving history, and payment information may only be used in AI tools approved for donor data. Generic drafting ("write a thank-you letter for a first-time donor") is fine; pasting donor records is not.

Client and beneficiary records receive our highest protection. Before any AI use involving client information — even de-identified — confirm the tool is approved for it and that identifying details are removed.

De-identification means removing names, contact details, ID numbers, exact dates, and any combination of details that could identify a person in context. Small-community details can identify someone even without a name.
Financial data may be used only in approved tools. Bank details, payment card data, and account credentials must never be entered into any AI tool.

When an approved tool offers privacy controls — such as turning off training on our data or setting retention limits — {OWNER_ROLE} configures them to the most protective practical setting before the tool is used.
AI outputs derived from our data are records. Store meaningful outputs in our systems, not in personal accounts, and apply our normal retention rules to them.

If we receive a request to delete someone's data, that deletion extends to copies held in AI tools where we control them. Tools that cannot honor deletion should not hold personal data in the first place.
{ORG} maintains a list of approved AI tools and what each is approved for. The list, kept by {OWNER_ROLE}, states which categories of information may be used with each tool.

Work involving anything beyond public information must use organization-managed accounts, not personal AI accounts. Personal accounts lack our privacy settings, and work product in them is invisible to the organization.
To request a new tool or a new use of an existing tool, ask {OWNER_ROLE}. Requests are reviewed promptly for privacy, security, cost, and fit; the default answer to low-risk requests is yes.
Free tools are not free: the payment is usually data. Free-tier AI tools are approved only where their data practices have been reviewed, and never for sensitive information.

AI features that appear inside software we already use — email, documents, databases, donor systems — are covered by this policy just like standalone tools, and are enabled or disabled deliberately, not by default.

The approved-tools list records, for each tool: approved uses, permitted data categories, account type, the privacy settings applied, and the date of last review. Entries are re-reviewed at least annually.
Only tools on the approved list may be used for any {ORG} work. Use of unlisted tools, on any account, is a policy violation.
A person is accountable for every piece of work at {ORG}, whether or not AI helped produce it. "The AI did it" is never an explanation.
{OWNER_ROLE} is responsible for this policy: keeping the approved-tools list, answering questions, reviewing requests, and coordinating the response when something goes wrong.

Where AI informs decisions about people — eligibility, prioritization, assessments — the process must include a meaningful human review step where a qualified person can see the AI's input, disagree with it, and decide differently.
Review must be real, not a rubber stamp. The reviewer must have the time, the access, and the authority to reject AI output. If review becomes clicking approve, the process gets redesigned.

Watch for bias. AI tools can reproduce and amplify unfair patterns, and the communities we serve are often the ones harmed. Outputs affecting people are checked for uneven impact, and concerns go to {OWNER_ROLE}.
For recurring AI-assisted processes that affect people, {OWNER_ROLE} periodically samples outcomes to check quality and fairness, and keeps brief notes of what was checked and found.

Significant new AI uses — new data categories, client-facing functions, or decision-support roles — require a short written assessment of benefits, risks, and safeguards before launch, approved by {OWNER_ROLE}.
We are honest about AI use. If asked whether AI was involved in producing something, we answer truthfully.

Content that is substantially AI-generated and published with little human editing is labeled as AI-assisted. Routine AI help with drafting and editing, where a person shapes the final product, does not require a label.
When people interact directly with an AI system we provide — such as a chatbot or automated assistant — they are told clearly that it is AI, and a route to a human is always available.
We do not use AI-generated imagery or stories presented as real clients or real events. Composite or illustrative material is labeled as such.

Funders, partners, and auditors who ask about our AI practices receive a straight answer, including this policy on request. If a funder's rules restrict AI use in work they fund, those rules are followed for that work.

Before adopting an AI tool or a vendor whose product includes AI, we review: what data it collects, where the data goes, whether our data trains their models, how we can get data out, and what it costs at real usage levels.
Vendor contracts for tools that touch personal data should state that our data is not used to train the vendor's models, is deleted on termination, and is protected by appropriate security measures.
When existing vendors add AI features to products we already use, those features get the same review as a new tool before we turn them on.
We ask vendors how their AI systems were evaluated for accuracy and bias, and prefer vendors who can answer. Silence on that question is information.
AI spending is tracked like any other software cost, reviewed annually against actual value, and consolidated where tools duplicate each other.
Everyone covered by this policy receives a basic orientation to it: what is encouraged, what is prohibited, and where to ask questions. New staff and volunteers receive it during onboarding.
Staff who use AI regularly receive practical training for their roles — effective prompting, verifying outputs, and the data rules for the tools they use.
Questions about AI are welcome and answered without judgment. It is always better to ask before trying something than to apologize after.
{ORG} maintains simple internal guidance — approved tools, example prompts, and dos and don'ts — kept current by {OWNER_ROLE} so good practice is easy to find.

If sensitive data is entered into an unapproved tool, or AI output causes harm or embarrassment, report it to {OWNER_ROLE} immediately. Fast reporting limits damage; honest mistakes reported promptly are treated as learning, not misconduct.

An AI incident includes: sensitive data disclosure to a tool, publication of significantly wrong AI-generated content, a decision improperly delegated to AI, or discovery of biased or harmful outputs.
On a report, {OWNER_ROLE} coordinates the response: contain the issue, assess who is affected, correct the record, notify affected people where appropriate, and meet any legal notification duties.
Incidents and near-misses are logged briefly — what happened, response, and what changed to prevent recurrence. The log informs policy reviews and, for significant incidents, board reporting.
This policy is reviewed at least annually, and sooner when laws change, we adopt significantly new AI uses, or an incident reveals a gap. {OWNER_ROLE} owns the review.
Staff feedback is part of every review: what is working, what is unclear, and where the policy blocks legitimate work. The policy serves the mission, not the reverse.
Each revision records its date and a short note of what changed. The current version is easy to find; superseded versions are retained.
This policy takes effect on adoption by {ORG}'s leadership or board and remains in effect until revised or replaced.

Health information addendum: {ORG} handles health information and treats it under the strictest rules in this policy. Protected health information (PHI) may not be entered into any AI tool unless that tool is covered by a business associate agreement (BAA) and approved in writing for PHI.

Consumer AI tools do not sign BAAs. Assume no general-purpose chatbot is ever approved for PHI, including "just a quick summary" of a client's situation. De-identified health data may be used only after identifiers are removed per our de-identification standard.
Suspected disclosure of PHI to an unapproved AI tool is treated as a potential breach: report immediately to {OWNER_ROLE}, who assesses it under our HIPAA breach procedures and notification duties.

Student and minor records addendum: records about students and minors receive heightened protection. Education records and any identifying information about minors may not be entered into AI tools that are not approved for them, and parental or guardian consent rules are respected for any AI use involving a child's information.
Online AI tools directed at or used with children under 13 raise additional obligations (COPPA). No AI tool is put in front of children in our programs without review and approval by {OWNER_ROLE}.

EU addendum: because {ORG} operates in the EU or handles data of EU residents, we act as a responsible deployer of AI systems: we use AI within providers' stated intended purposes, ensure human oversight of consequential uses, and keep basic records of significant AI systems in use.
Personal data of EU residents is handled per our data-protection obligations (GDPR), including lawful basis, minimization, and deletion rights, which apply fully to data used with AI tools.

Colorado addendum: Colorado law imposes duties on organizations deploying high-risk AI systems — systems that substantially shape consequential decisions about people. If any {ORG} AI use could be high-risk in this sense, {OWNER_ROLE} ensures the required care, review, and notice obligations are addressed before use.

State privacy addendum: one or more states where {ORG} operates have comprehensive consumer-privacy laws. Where they apply to us, individuals' rights — access, correction, deletion, and opt-outs — extend to personal data used with AI tools, and our vendor contracts reflect these duties.

Values addendum: AI use at {ORG} is consistent with our faith and values. Tools assist our people; they do not replace human presence in ministry, pastoral care, or community relationships. Content representing our beliefs and teaching is always reviewed by appropriate leadership before use.
Pastoral conversations and matters shared in spiritual confidence are never entered into AI tools. That confidence is absolute and is not affected by any tool approval elsewhere in this policy.

Grantmaking addendum: AI may assist with sorting, summarizing, and preparing grant applications for review, but funding decisions are made by people. No application is declined based on AI assessment without human review of that application.
{ORG} states clearly in its application materials whether and how AI is used in reviewing applications, and what applicants may or may not use AI for in preparing them.

Advocacy addendum: AI-assisted advocacy content is held to a strict accuracy standard. Claims about policies, laws, or opponents' positions are verified against primary sources; fabricated or misattributed material is never used, whatever its origin.
